title: Lior and the Choir
premise: Tamsin Brightwater carves bone charms in a valley where magic cannot enter, and only there can he hear the dead clearly enough to give them rest. When a dying courier leaves him a map to the capital and a plea to unbind King Aldric from the Hollow Choir—a chorus of dead voices that has worn the crown for a decade—Tamsin's safe invisibility ends, because the Choir hears him back and wants his gift silenced. Guided by the map, hunted by the king's Justiciars, and shadowed by the loyal soldier Sera Vane who must choose between her oath and the truth, Tamsin learns the Choir was built from murdered singers whose deaths the court buried. In the throne room, Tamsin cannot destroy the Choir without killing the king it animates; instead he frees the singers' voices by singing their true names, letting justice fall outside the law as the crown—and the king—crumbles, leaving Sera to carry the truth home while Tamsin returns to a valley that no longer feels like refuge.
about_author: Ivo Eriksen is the pen name of a former church organist who grew up in a Norwegian fishing village where old songs were said to keep the sea calm. They write fantasy about music, memory, and the price of being believed.

chapters.title: The Valley That Refuses Magic
chapters.summary: Tamsin Brightwater carves a charm for a grieving mother, hearing her drowned son's last words through the bone. The valley's magic-dead silence is what lets the dead speak cleanly, and Tamsin treasures his small, hidden life. POV: Tamsin. Beat: quiet competence shadowed by loneliness—the calm before the map arrives.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Ford
chapters.summary: A bloodied courier collapses at the valley ford, pressing a wax-sealed map into Tamsin's hands and gasping about 'the thing wearing the king.' The valley's wardens want him gone before he dies inside the border; Tamsin hears the man's dead voice beg him not to open the map. POV: Tamsin. Beat: dread and reluctant responsibility.

chapters.title: What the Dead Man Knew
chapters.summary: The courier dies at dusk, and his ghost lingers long enough to warn Tamsin: the Hollow Choir sings through King Aldric, and anyone who hears its true names becomes prey. Tamsin burns nothing, tells no one, but the map won't stay shut—it hums. POV: Tamsin. Beat: the moment staying invisible stops being possible.

chapters.title: Leaving Brightwater
chapters.summary: Tamsin slips out past the wardens with his carving tools and his grandmother's tuning fork, the only object that ever left the valley and came back unchanged. Behind him, for the first time in years, he hears faint singing on the wind. POV: Tamsin. Beat: grief for the life he's abandoning, fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Road of Small Kings
chapters.summary: On the trade road Tamsin passes villages where shrines stand defaced and bells hang silent; the Crown has been 'harmonizing' local rites for a decade. He realizes the Choir isn't just haunting the palace—it's eating the country's older voices. POV: Tamsin. Beat: dawning scale of the threat.

chapters.title: Sera Vane Takes the Road
chapters.summary: Justiciar-sergeant Sera Vane, sent to recover the courier's map, tracks Tamsin to an inn and finds instead a room full of travelers who all heard singing in their sleep. She reports nothing yet, unsettled: her orders smell wrong. POV: Sera. Beat: loyalty beginning to itch against doubt.

chapters.title: The Inn of Nine Bells
chapters.summary: Sera corners Tamsin; he proves what he is by relaying her dead brother's message, which she never told anyone. Instead of arresting him, she strikes a wary bargain—she'll get him to the capital if he confirms whether the king is truly king. POV: alternating Tamsin/Sera. Beat: distrust becoming alliance.

chapters.title: Hunted Through the Marshes
chapters.summary: Choir-bound hunters—men whose eyes sing when they blink—ambush them in the fens. Tamsin discovers the tuning fork disrupts the hunters' song, shattering their obedience for precious seconds. They escape, barely, and Sera sees the Court's hand in the ambush. POV: Sera. Beat: terror, and the first crack in her faith in the law.

chapters.title: The City That Hums
chapters.summary: The capital greets them with beauty and wrongness: every street performer plays the same melody, every bell tower rings slightly flat. Tamsin's skull aches; the Choir is vast here, and it has noticed him arriving. POV: Tamsin. Beat: awe curdling into claustrophobia.

chapters.title: An Audience of Ash
chapters.summary: Using Sera's credentials, they glimpse King Aldric at a ceremony—his mouth moving in perfect unison with a hundred courtiers, all singing under their breath. Tamsin hears beneath it the screams of the original singers. POV: Tamsin. Beat: horror confirmed; the enemy has a face.

chapters.title: The Archivist of Suppressed Songs
chapters.summary: In the undercroft archives, blind archivist Maren Corvane keeps banned hymnals. She reveals the Choir's origin: twelve royal choristers murdered after discovering the old king's crimes, their voices bound as instruments of rule. POV: Maren. Beat: revelation—the dead were victims first, weapons second.

chapters.title: Names in Bone
chapters.summary: Maren gives Tamsin a reliquary of the choristers' finger bones; carved with their true names, they could unbind the Choir—but only if spoken aloud in the Choir's own presence, which will kill the speaker. Tamsin begins carving anyway. POV: Tamsin. Beat: acceptance of sacrifice; craft as courage.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Bell Tower
chapters.summary: Sera's superior, High Justiciar Ossler, confronts her: he knows everything and offers her promotion for delivering Tamsin. She stalls, then warns Tamsin—openly choosing truth over oath. POV: Sera. Beat: the theme made flesh; loyalty redefined.

chapters.title: The Choir Finds His Name
chapters.summary: The Choir speaks to Tamsin directly through a street child's mouth, offering to return his valley's peace if he surrenders the bones—and showing him visions of Brightwater already burning. It lies, but the lie nearly works. POV: Tamsin. Beat: temptation and despair at their lowest point.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Ossler raids the archive; Maren dies buying time, pressing the final name into Tamsin's memory. Sera is branded traitor, and the two flee the city walls as wanted criminals with nowhere left to run but the palace itself. POV: Sera. Beat: grief, guilt, and grim commitment.

chapters.title: The Old Song Under the City
chapters.summary: Following the map's hidden route, they find the sealed crypt where the twelve choristers were buried unnamed. There the dead themselves speak—not begging rescue, but asking to be remembered rightly before they're freed. POV: Tamsin. Beat: the mission changes from escape to witness.

chapters.title: Doors of the Throne Hall
chapters.summary: Midwinter court approaches; the Choir will renew its binding before the assembled nobility. Sera uses her last shred of rank to get them into the ceremony as musicians. Tamsin hides the carved bones inside his instrument case. POV: Sera. Beat: coiled tension; no way out but through.

chapters.title: The Renewal
chapters.summary: Before the court, the Choir begins its renewal rite, and King Aldric's body moves like a puppet remembering its strings. Tamsin steps from the gallery and strikes the tuning fork—the hall's false harmony shatters, and every noble hears, for one raw second, the screaming underneath. POV: Tamsin. Beat: climax ignites; the lie exposed publicly.

chapters.title: Twelve True Names
chapters.summary: As guards close in, Tamsin sings the twelve names, each verse costing him breath, warmth, and finally his ability to hear any dead at all. The Choir unravels into twelve freed voices; the king collapses, briefly himself, whispering thanks before the vacancy of ten stolen years takes him. POV: Tamsin. Beat: sacrifice fulfilled; justice done outside any law.

chapters.title: After the Silence
chapters.summary: Sera stands before the stunned court and testifies to everything—Ossler's complicity, the murders, the cover-up—knowing the institution may destroy her for it. Some lords listen. The bells ring genuinely out of tune for the first time in a decade, and it sounds like honesty. POV: Sera. Beat: costly truth spoken; the law forced to reckon.

chapters.title: The Quiet Return
chapters.summary: Tamsin goes home deaf to the dead, mourning the loss like a severed limb—until he realizes he can now hear the living more clearly than ever. Brightwater's wardens ask what the world was like; he says the valley was never really hiding him, only keeping him. POV: Tamsin. Beat: bittersweet restoration; identity remade.

chapters.title: Coda: What the Bells Remember
chapters.summary: Months later, Sera arrives in the valley carrying Maren's restored archive and a summons: the new regency wants a bone-carver who understands how power sings. Tamsin looks at the road, then at his tools, and begins packing—this time by choice. POV: Tamsin. Beat: resolution with an open door; the watcher becomes the walker.
